title: Temple of Olympian Zeus and Hadrian's Arch

start.label: supported
start.says: An earlier temple was built by the tyrant Peisistratus around 550 BC; his sons began the colossal new one around 520 BC.
quote: An earlier temple had stood there, constructed by the tyrant Peisistratus around 550 BC.
the construction of a colossal new Temple of Olympian Zeus was begun around 520 BC by his sons, Hippias and Hipparchos

greatest.label: supported
greatest.says: The tyrants meant it to be the greatest temple in the ancient world.
quote: who envisioned building the greatest temple in the ancient world

stalled.label: supported
stalled.says: Only the platform and parts of columns were done, and it stayed that way for 336 years.
quote: Only the platform and some elements of the columns had been completed by that point, and the temple remained in that state for 336 years.

sulla.label: supported
sulla.says: The Roman general Sulla took some unfinished columns to Rome.
quote: Sulla seized some of the incomplete columns and transported them to Rome

hadrian.label: supported
hadrian.says: Emperor Hadrian finally completed and dedicated it in 132 AD, about 638 years after it began.
quote: the temple was formally dedicated by Hadrian in 132
the project was finally completed, around 638 years after it had begun

size.label: supported
size.says: It had 104 columns, each about 17 m high, and was the largest temple in Greece in Roman times.
quote: for a total of 104 columns, each 17.25 m high
was renowned as the largest temple in Greece

statue.label: supported
statue.says: The cella held a gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus and a statue of Hadrian.
quote: The cella housed a chryselephantine statue of Zeus and a statue of Hadrian, who was honoured alongside the god.

1436.label: supported
1436.says: By 1436 a visitor found only 21 of the 104 columns standing.
quote: visited Athens in 1436 he found only 21 of the original 104 columns still standing

1759.label: supported
1759.says: An inscription on a surviving column records that on 27 April 1759 a column was pulled down.
quote: which states that "on 27 April 1759 he pulled down the column"

tzistarakis.label: disputed
tzistarakis.says: A chronicler says governor Tzistarakis blew up a column to make plaster for his mosque; another account says it was more likely a column of Hadrian's Library.
quote: who is recorded by a chronicler as having "destroyed one of Hadrian's columns with gunpowder" in order to re-use the marble to make plaster for the Tzistarakis Mosque
although it is more likely that he used one of the columns of the nearby Hadrian's Library

storm.label: supported
storm.says: Fifteen columns stand today; a sixteenth fell in a storm in 1852.
quote: Fifteen columns remain standing today and a sixteenth column lies on the ground where it fell during a storm in 1852.

arch-why.label: disputed
arch-why.says: The arch may have been built to celebrate Hadrian, around the dedication in 131 or 132 AD.
quote: It has been proposed that the arch was built to celebrate the adventus (arrival) of the Roman emperor Hadrian and to honor him for his many benefactions to the city, on the occasion of the dedication of the nearby temple complex in 131 or 132 AD.

arch-nw.label: supported
arch-nw.says: The side facing the Acropolis reads: this is Athens, the ancient city of Theseus.
quote: On the northwest side (towards the Acropolis), the inscription was: ΑΙΔ' ΕΙΣΙΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙ ΘΗΣΕΩΣ Η ΠΡΙΝ ΠΟΛΙΣ (this is Athens, the ancient city of Theseus).

arch-se.label: supported
arch-se.says: The side facing the temple reads: this is the city of Hadrian, and not of Theseus.
quote: The inscription on the southeast side (facing the Olympeion) reads: ΑΙΔ' ΕΙΣ' ΑΔΡΙΑΝΟΥ ΚΟΥΧΙ ΘΗΣΕΩΣ ΠΟΛΙΣ (this is the city of Hadrian, and not of Theseus).

arch-who.label: disputed
arch-who.says: It is not certain who commissioned the arch; probably the citizens of Athens.
quote: It is not certain who commissioned the arch, although it is probable that it was the citizens of Athens.

arch-carved.label: supported
arch-carved.says: Two inscriptions are carved over the opening, one on each side.
quote: Two inscriptions are carved on the architrave of the arch’s lower level, one centered over the arched opening on either side.

antiochus.label: supported
antiochus.says: In 174 BC Antiochus IV restarted the project; it halted again at his death in 164 BC.
quote: It was not until 174 BC that the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes
revived the project
the project ground to a halt again in 164 BC with the death of Antiochus

arch-meaning.label: disputed
arch-meaning.says: It is uncertain whether the inscriptions mean the whole city or an old and new part.
quote: it is uncertain whether they refer to the city as a whole or to the city in two parts: one old and one new

parts.name: Hadrian's Arch
parts.stand: On the pavement beside the marble arch, well back from the kerb of busy Amalias Avenue.

paras.t: This marble gateway is Hadrian's Arch. Over the opening, on each side, a line of Greek is carved. On the side facing the Acropolis, it says: this is Athens, the ancient city of Theseus.

The other side, facing the temple, says: this is the city of Hadrian, and not of Theseus. Quite a compliment to a Roman emperor. Nobody knows for certain who put the arch up, but it was probably the citizens of Athens.
Historians aren't sure what the words mean: the whole city, or an old part and a new part. The arch itself was probably put up to honour Hadrian around AD 131 or 132.

parts.name: The temple that took six centuries
parts.stand: Inside the site, at the end of the path where the tall columns stand in a group.

paras.t: Now look at those giant columns. This was meant to be the greatest temple in the ancient world, for Zeus, king of the gods. Its story is one of the great builders' sagas.

Around 550 BC the tyrant Peisistratus built a temple here, and around 520 BC his sons started this enormous one. Then it stalled. Only the platform and parts of the columns were done, and it sat that way for 336 years. In 174 BC a Greek king, Antiochus the Fourth, restarted the work, until his death in 164 BC stopped it again. Then the Roman general Sulla carried off some of the unfinished columns to Rome.

Finally the emperor Hadrian finished it and dedicated it in AD 132, more than six centuries after it was started. It had 104 columns, each about 17 metres tall, the largest temple in Greece. Inside stood a gold-and-ivory Zeus, and next to the god, a statue of Hadrian himself.

parts.name: What happened to the columns
parts.stand: Stand where you can see the single column lying on the ground in pieces.

paras.t: So where did 104 columns go? By 1436 a traveller counted only 21 standing. Over the centuries the marble was simply taken.

One loss is written on the stone itself. An inscription on a surviving column records that on 27 April 1759 a column was pulled down. A chronicler blamed the Ottoman governor, Tzistarakis, who wanted marble for plaster for his new mosque. Another account says it was more likely a column from Hadrian's Library. Either way, his mosque still stands in Monastiraki.
Fifteen columns stand today. The one lying in pieces at your feet came down in a storm in 1852. It's the clearest sense you'll get of just how huge they are.

practical.t: Hours and tickets change by season. Check the official ticket site before you go. The arch is on the street and can be seen at any time.
